visits.text: Forget everything you've seen since the start of the trip. In an hour's flight from Bora Bora, the landscape shifts: volcanic peaks disappear, the horizon flattens, and suddenly there's nothing but water—blue in every direction. Then a line of sand and coconut palms appears, barely higher than the waves. Welcome to an atoll. Rangiroa is the world's second largest: its lagoon is 80 km long and 30 wide. From the shore, you can't see the other side.

Avatoru village stretches along a strip of land so narrow you can see the lagoon on one side and the ocean on the other. A few colorful houses, a coral church, dogs asleep on the road—the rhythm of life here follows the tides.

Walk to Tiputa Pass, east of the village. It's a 200-meter-wide channel where the lagoon current meets the ocean. From the edge, you can watch spinner dolphins surfing the current in late afternoon—they come by the dozens.

The small Tiputa lighthouse, at the entrance to the pass, is reached by boat from the Avatoru motu. It offers a viewpoint over the dolphins' ballet and the changing colors of the current—sometimes deep blue, sometimes emerald green, depending on the tide.

Full-day excursion to the Blue Lagoon, an hour by boat southwest of Avatoru. It's a lagoon within the lagoon—a natural basin bounded by a chain of motus where the water is an almost unreal pale blue. The white sand bottom lies 1 meter below the surface for hundreds of meters.

Île aux Récifs, in the south of the atoll, is a lunar landscape: fossilized coral formations sculpted by erosion form mushrooms, arches, and labyrinths of gray stone in the middle of the lagoon. It looks like a garden of natural sculptures.
Stop at a deserted motu with pink sand beaches—the color comes from red coral fragments mixed with white sand. The place is completely wild, with no buildings.

Rangiroa is home to a vineyard—yes, wine on a Pacific atoll. The estate produces white and rosé wine from grape varieties adapted to the tropical climate. The vines grow on coral sand and yield two harvests per year. The visit is short but surprising.

Visit to a pearl farm on the atoll. The grafting technician shows you how they insert a nucleus into the Pinctada margaritifera oyster, then explains the 18-month wait before harvest. Tuamotu pearl oysters produce pearls with green, eggplant, and peacock overtones—different from Society Islands pearls.

Walk along the reef on the ocean side, between Avatoru and Tiputa. The road crosses coconut groves and runs along deserted beaches beaten by the swell. The contrast between the lagoon's calm and the ocean's power is striking.

activities.text: Drift snorkeling in Tiputa Pass (with a guide). The current carries you through the channel among Napoleon wrasses, jacks, barracudas, and sometimes gray reef sharks. It's impressive but supervised—the guide chooses the timing based on the current.

Dinner of grilled fish at a local guesthouse. The atolls depend on fishing—the fish is ultra-fresh, prepared simply with lime and coconut milk. Try the marinated raw bluefin tuna, a Tuamotu specialty.

Swimming and snorkeling in the Blue Lagoon: juvenile blacktip reef sharks swim in the shallow water between your legs. They measure 40–60 cm and are harmless—children love it. Mask and snorkel provided by the operator.

Barbecue lunch on a motu: the guide prepares grilled fish over a coconut wood fire, accompanied by coconut milk rice and tropical fruits. You eat with your feet in the sand, alone in the middle of the Pacific.

Scuba diving at Avatoru Pass—Rangiroa's second major dive site. You'll encounter schools of jacks, gray reef sharks, Napoleon wrasses, and sometimes hammerhead sharks between December and March. Even for experienced divers, it's a highlight.
Last evening on the atoll. The Tuamotu sky, free from light pollution, is one of Polynesia's most beautiful for stargazing. The Milky Way is visible to the naked eye.

visits.text: The village of Fare, on Huahine Nui's west coast, is the arrival point on the island. A few streets lined with craft shops, a small harbor, and a white sand beach facing the lagoon—the atmosphere is that of a Polynesian village frozen in time. No traffic lights, no luxury resorts: Huahine cultivates its wild side.

Take the road to Maeva village in the island's northeast. It's the largest archaeological site in French Polynesia: about forty marae (stone temples) stretch between Matairea hill and the shores of Lake Fauna Nui. Panels explain the function of each structure—some served for ceremonies, others for the investiture of chiefs.

At the edge of Lake Fauna Nui, you'll see the stone fish traps, restored and still used by locals. These basalt enclosures date back several centuries—fish enter with the rising tide and are trapped at low tide. An ingenious technique that still works today.

The community museum of Fare Pote'e, a large traditional house rebuilt on stilts at the lake's edge, displays archaeological objects found at the Maeva site: mother-of-pearl fishhooks, basalt adzes, and bone ornaments.

Huahine is actually two islands—Huahine Nui to the north and Huahine Iti to the south—linked by a bridge at Maroe. Cross this bridge and head south: vegetation thickens, dwellings become scarce, the road follows an increasingly wild lagoon.

Avea Bay, on the southwestern coast of Huahine Iti, is one of Polynesia's most beautiful anchorages. Allow for a round trip by road from Fare. White sand, coconut palms leaning over the water, and a shallow lagoon shifting from emerald green to cobalt blue. Few people—the opposite of Bora Bora.

Marae Anini, at the southern tip of Huahine Iti, extends onto a rocky cape facing the ocean. Allow for a round trip by road from Fare. This basalt stone temple was used for ceremonies connected with navigation—fitting for an island from which large canoes set out for the Leeward Islands.

Head back up the east coast through the village of Parea; allow for a round trip by road from Fare for this outing. The gardens overflow with breadfruit trees, papaya trees and banana plants. If you meet a resident, there is a good chance they will offer you a grapefruit—hospitality on Huahine is no myth.

Take the east coast road, less frequented than the west. After about ten kilometers, Faie village is home to a stream where blue-eyed eels live, considered sacred by locals. They sometimes measure over a meter and will eat from your hand—a strange and slightly intimidating spectacle.

Continue to Bourayne Bay, nestled between two hills covered in dense vegetation. No beach here, but a viewpoint above that overlooks the entire bay and the lagoon beyond. It's the kind of place where you sit for ten minutes and stay an hour.

Return along the inner coast through the plantations. Huahine grows vanilla, noni, watermelon, and melon in open fields—roadside stalls sell fruit picked that morning. Stop, chat, buy a bunch of bananas for next to nothing.

activities.text: Canoe tour on Huahine Nui's lagoon. The water is deep blue on the pass side and translucent turquoise on the motu side. You'll likely encounter rays and green turtles—Huahine is one of the islands where they're most common.
Late afternoon, settle on Fare beach for sunset. Fishing canoes return to port, children play in the warm water—a quiet moment, far from Bora Bora's tourist bustle.

Snorkeling in the lagoon of Avea Bay; allow for a round trip by road from Fare. The water is calm and shallow, and the corals are in good condition. Parrotfish, damselfish and sometimes green turtles grazing on seagrass. A mask and snorkel are enough.

Island tour by bike or scooter. Huahine is about 30 km around—allow half a day by bike with stops. The road is flat and shaded, and you'll pass through sleepy villages and coconut groves, with viewpoints over the lagoon along the way.

This is a day to take a breather. No tight schedule—settle on Fare beach with a book, swim when the mood strikes, watch fishing canoes return in early afternoon. Huahine is meant to be savored slowly, and that's precisely why you come.

Late afternoon, walk to Fare wharf for sunset. Locals gather there, some fishing from the dock, children jumping in the water. If a local offers you a taste of poisson cru they've just prepared, don't refuse.

visits.text: The ferry crosses the Vaiare pass and reveals Moorea, Tahiti's sister island. As soon as you dock, the trident-shaped silhouette of its mountains towers above: Cook's Bay to the left, Opunohu Bay to the right, separated by sacred Mount Rotui (899 m).

Drive up the shaded little road to the Opunohu Lookout, at 240 meters altitude in the heart of a 9-km-diameter crater. The 360° panorama embraces both bays, eight mountain ranges, the lagoon and the pineapple fields below.

On the way back down, stop at the Opunohu agricultural school. Students produce tropical fruit jams and pineapple juice from the valley. Archaeological sites (marae) lie nearby along the marked trail.
Marae Titiroa, a Polynesian temple of basalt stones nestled in the vegetation of Opunohu Valley, bears witness to the ancient Ma'ohi religion. Explanatory panels line the site.
The public beach of Ta'ahiamanu in Opunohu Bay unfurls a strip of white sand bordered by coconut trees. The shallow, calm water makes it a family-friendly swimming spot.
Te Fare Natura, Moorea's eco-museum, sits at the exit of Opunohu Bay. Interactive exhibits on reef ecosystems, endemic fauna and the island's volcanic geology.
Make a detour via the "Magic Mountain" for a stunning viewpoint over the turquoise lagoon on the west side. Access is via a short but steep track.
Temae Beach, in the northeast near the airport, is one of the most beautiful in Polynesia. Pristine white sand, crystal-clear waters and a direct view of Tahiti in the distance.
The Manutea fruit juice distillery-factory, located in Opunohu Bay, processes pineapples and local fruits. Free tasting of artisanal juices, liqueurs and jams.
In the mood for a cultural show? Polynesian evenings offered on the island combine a ma'a tahiti buffet, traditional dances, percussion and fire show under the stars.

activities.text: Snorkeling in the lagoon on the Cook's Bay side: butterflyfish, surgeonfish and small stingrays glide above corals accessible from the beach. Mornings offer optimal visibility.
Lagoon boat tour between the two bays. You navigate at the foot of Mount Rotui, encounter stingrays and small blacktip reef sharks in the shallow waters around the motus.
Hike to the Three Coconuts Pass starting from the Opunohu Lookout. The trail crosses dense tropical forest and emerges at a pass with views over both bays and the lagoon on the Haapiti side.
Polynesian cooking class: preparing raw fish with lime and coconut milk, the fenua's signature dish. Some guesthouses offer this workshop.

places.name: Papeete

visits.text: Papeete's market, Mapuru a Paraita, occupies a two-story covered building right in the city center. Vanilla, handmade monoï oil, fresh tiare flower crowns, and colorful tifaifai quilts pile high on the stalls. Sunday mornings from 4 a.m. onward, Tahitian families flood the aisles—it's the most authentic time to visit.

Step inside Notre-Dame Cathedral, recognizable by its bright yellow facade and bell tower dominating downtown. Construction began in 1856 and was completed in 1875; the cathedral houses stained glass windows that filter the tropical light and offers welcome coolness.
Head to Paofai Gardens along the waterfront. This tree-lined promenade facing the harbor offers an unobstructed view of Moorea's silhouette. Outrigger canoe (va'a) crews train here in late afternoon.
The Pearl Museum traces the history of pearl farming in French Polynesia. In 45 minutes, you'll learn to distinguish the luster, orient, and shapes of Tahitian black pearls.
Walk up Boulevard Pomaré to spot the street art murals created during the Ono'u festival. International artists have transformed several downtown facades into an open-air gallery.

The three Faarumai waterfalls are at PK 22 on the east coast, 22 km from Papeete. The first, Vaimahuta, plunges 80 meters down a basalt wall—five minutes' walk from the parking area. The other two, Haamaremare Rahi and Iti, require an additional 20 minutes on a steeper trail.

Stop at the Arahoho Blowhole, just beside the waterfalls. The ocean rushes into a lava tube carved by erosion beneath the road and shoots a powerful jet of water landward. In Tahitian, Arahoho means “the road that roars.” The spectacle depends on the swell: the stronger it is, the more impressive the blast.
Take the coastal road to Pointe Vénus in Mahina (PK 10). The white 25-meter lighthouse, built in 1867, marks where Europeans landed in 1767. Black sand beach and views of Moorea at sunset.
The Tahara'a lookout, at the start of the east coast as you leave Papeete, offers a panorama of the lagoon, the barrier reef, and the Tahiti Iti peninsula from its viewing terrace.

The Museum of Tahiti and Her Islands in Punaauia on the west coast (PK 15) traces the natural and cultural history of Polynesia. Collections of tapa cloth, traditional canoes, and basalt tools. Check opening days before visiting.

Back on Tahiti for the final two days, head toward the peninsula (Tahiti Iti), often overlooked by visitors. Allow for a round trip by road from Papeete. The Taravao isthmus connects the island's two parts—beyond it, the road narrows, the vegetation thickens and the tourists disappear.

Marae Arahurahu, in Paea (PK 22.5 on the west coast), is Tahiti's best-restored marae. Allow for a round trip by road from Papeete. Its terraced stone platform, surrounded by coconut palms, still hosts reenactments of traditional ceremonies.
The Maraa caves, hollowed into the coastal cliff in Paea, shelter pools of crystal-clear fresh water amid ferns. Allow for a round trip by road from Papeete. A quick and surprising stop.

Head up to the Taravao plateau, at an altitude of 600 meters; allow for a round trip by road from Papeete. The road winds through pastures (yes, cows on Tahiti) and opens onto a panorama taking in the whole northern coast, the lagoon and Moorea in the distance. In clear weather, it is one of the island's most beautiful viewpoints.

Head back down toward the south coast and the village of Teahupo'o, famous in the surfing world for its legendary wave; allow for a round trip by road from Papeete for this outing. There is not much to see from the shore—the wave forms on the reef, 500 meters offshore. But the village itself, tucked between the mountain and lagoon, is worth visiting for its atmosphere.

Continue to the end of the road on the east side, toward the village of Tautira; allow for a round trip by road from Papeete for this outing. The road ends there—beyond lies the Pari cliff, accessible only on foot or by boat. The village is quiet, bordered by a river and a sheltered lagoon.

Last morning in Papeete. Return to the market—not to buy this time, but to observe. The first day you were a tourist; twenty days later you recognize the flowers, fruits, smells. The tiare crown seller greets you because she's seen you pass three times. That's the measure of a journey: the way you see things has changed.

King Pomare V's tomb in Arue on the east coast is the resting place of Tahiti's last king, who died in 1891. The white coral monument topped with a funerary urn overlooks the lagoon—a quiet and somewhat melancholic place, reflecting a kingdom that quietly faded away.

If your flight is in the evening (many international flights depart at night), save the afternoon for the beach at PK 18 in Punaauia. White sand, calm water, Moorea opposite—it's your last image of Polynesia, might as well make it beautiful.

activities.text: The food trucks at Place Vaiete set up every evening from 6 p.m. facing the harbor. Raw fish with coconut milk, chow mein, grilled freshwater shrimp—a local institution under the stars.
If you arrive on a Sunday, head to Paofai Protestant Temple to hear the polyphonic religious singing. Worshippers wear hats and white outfits—a unique sonic and visual experience.
Swimming at a black sand beach along the east coast. The water is warm year-round but currents can be strong—respect the flags and stick to supervised areas.
Vaiava Beach (PK 18, Punaauia) offers white sand on the west side and easy snorkeling above coral heads, with direct views of Moorea.

Swimming in the Teahupo'o lagoon, on the inside (not the wave side); allow for a round trip by road from Papeete. The water is calm and warm, with a sandy bottom. Some operators offer boat trips to see the wave closer up—even without surfing, the swell rising over the reef is an impressive sight.
Lunch at a local peninsula snack bar: raw fish, ma'a tinito (a Chinese-Tahitian dish), or steak and fries—everyday Tahitian cooking, far from tourist restaurants.

Last-minute shopping at the market or downtown shops: vanilla pods, handmade monoï, hand-painted pareos. Fresh tiare crowns won't survive the journey, but their fragrance on the plane makes them worth buying.
Transfer to Faa'a airport, 5 km from Papeete. Arrive with time to spare—check-in for international flights opens 3 hours before departure. The last Polynesian sunset is visible from the tarmac.

visits.text: Fakarava is an atoll classified as a UNESCO biosphere reserve—one of the few in the world. Sixty kilometers long and 25 wide, it's pierced by two passes that rank among the planet's best dive sites.

Rotoava village, in the atoll's northeast, is Fakarava's only real village. A few hundred inhabitants, a white coral church, houses on stilts, and a fishing wharf. The church, built entirely of coral blocks by missionaries, is worth a stop for its unique architecture.

The north pass, Garuae, is Polynesia's widest—an opening 1,600 meters wide. From the shore, you see the current tracing turquoise lines in the darker water. Sharks, rays, dolphins, and schools of tuna pass through here.
Walk along the lagoon shore, south of Rotoava. The sand is white, scattered with shells and polished coral pieces. Not a sound, not a building—just the lagoon, coconut palms, and wind.

Full-day excursion to the south pass, Tumakohua, at the atoll's opposite end. The boat journey takes about 1.5 hours and crosses the full length of the lagoon—an expanse of turquoise water as far as the eye can see.

The abandoned village of Tetamanu, beside the south pass, was once the atoll's capital. A coral church built in 1874 remains—tiny and moving, with rough wooden benches and an altar facing the sea. A few isolated guesthouses around the village have come back to life.

The south pass, narrower than Garuae (200 meters), concentrates marine life. This is where the famous “shark wall” forms—hundreds of gray reef sharks that gather in the pass current, especially on the rising tide.

Last morning on the atoll. Borrow a bike and ride along the Rotoava road—it runs just a few kilometers along the lagoon. You'll pass coconut groves where locals dry copra, coconut flesh cut and laid out in the sun. It's been the atoll's main economic resource for over a century, long before tourism.

At low tide, go down to the reef flat on the east side. You walk on an exposed reef dotted with pools where miniature worlds bustle—pencil urchins, giant clams with electric blue lips, sea stars, small trapped fish waiting for the tide. Take time to look: each pool is an aquarium.

Make a last stop at the northern point, where the reef meets the entrance to Garuae Pass. The current traces veins of color in the water—from jade green to midnight blue depending on depth and tide. It's the kind of view you watch for a long time, trying to memorize it.

activities.text: Guided snorkeling boat trip from Rotoava toward the lagoon-side entrance to Garuae Pass. The incoming current brings crystal-clear water and schools of tropical fish. Entering the water depends on conditions and the local guide's decision: do not enter the pass alone.
Sunset from Rotoava beach. With no land rising on the horizon, the sun plunges directly into the Pacific—a perfect orange disk that disappears in seconds.

Diving in Tumakohua Pass—THE dive site in Fakarava. You descend into the current amid 200 to 700 gray reef sharks. They're not interested in you—they're hunting in the current. It's a spectacle unique in the world, regularly ranked among the world's top 10 dives.

Lunch on the motu near Tetamanu, between two dives or while waiting for divers. Raw fish, coconut rice, fruit—the meal is simple and served under a fare (palm-leaf shelter) with your feet in the sand.

One last dive or guided snorkeling trip at Garuae, reached by boat from Rotoava, for those who want more. Otherwise, spend the morning in the lagoon water beside the village—knee-deep, with a sandy bottom and colorful corals within snorkeling reach. No boat or guide is needed for this swim beside the village.

In the Tuamotu Islands, if the sky is clear that evening, go outside after dinner: the Milky Way forms a complete arc from one horizon to the other, so dense that it casts a shadow. It may be the most memorable moment of the whole trip.

places.name: Uturoa

visits.text: Uturoa, Raiatea's main town, stretches along a quiet waterfront. Its small covered market sells fish, tropical fruits, and local crafts. The atmosphere is much calmer than in Papeete.

Marae Taputapuātea, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017, lies beside the lagoon at the southeastern tip of Raiatea. Allow for a round trip by road from Uturoa. Dedicated to the god 'Oro, this political, ceremonial and funerary center brought together chiefs from across the Polynesian Triangle. Several marae with distinct functions stand across a vast basalt stone site facing the sacred Te Ava Mo'a Pass.

Opposite the marae, the sacred mountain Tea'etapu overlooks the Opoa Valley. Allow for a round trip by road from Uturoa to the trailhead, followed by a walk toward the summit for a view down over the site, the lagoon and the ocean.

Raiatea is the cradle of Ma'ohi civilization: it's from this island that ancient Polynesian navigators set out to colonize Hawaii, New Zealand, and Easter Island. The Taputapuātea site remains a pilgrimage destination for Polynesians worldwide.

Taha'a, nicknamed the Vanilla Island, shares the same lagoon as Raiatea—30 minutes by boat is enough to reach it. The island produces about 80% of all French Polynesia's vanilla, the Vanilla tahitensis variety prized by chefs worldwide.

Visit to a vanilla plantation: cultivators explain the manual pollination of flowers, the harvest, and the long months of preparation needed to obtain the brown, fragrant pods. The sweet aroma permeates the greenhouse.

Stop at a family pearl farm to understand the grafting of Pinctada margaritifera oysters. Live demonstration and explanations on the classification of Tahitian black pearls—luster, orient, shape, and size.
Taha'a's rum distillery produces organic rhum agricole from sugarcane grown on former vanilla plots. Tasting available on-site.

activities.text: Trip upstream by boat or kayak on the Faaroa River, French Polynesia's only navigable river. The motorized canoe ventures into a lush jungle of tree ferns, sea hibiscus, and mape (Polynesian chestnut trees). The guide recounts legends of the valley.
Swimming and snorkeling at Motu Iriru or Ofetaro, two public islets in Raiatea's lagoon accessible by boat. White sand, crystal-clear water, and tropical fish.

Drift snorkeling in the coral garden of Motu Tau Tau, northwest of Taha'a. You let yourself be carried by the current above a natural aquarium of colorful corals, anemones, and tropical fish. Shallow, accessible to all.
Lunch on a deserted motu: Polynesian barbecue of grilled fish, cooked bananas, and coconut milk, feet in the white sand facing the turquoise lagoon.
Watching blacktip reef sharks in the shallows on the reef side. They swim in very shallow water and pose no danger—still, maintain a reasonable distance.

visits.text: The plane flies over Bora Bora's lagoon before landing on Motu Mute—the old airstrip built by the Americans in 1942. A boat shuttle connects to Vaitape, the island's main town.

Matira Beach, at the southern tip of the main island: a kilometer and a half of white sand edged with coconut palms. It's Bora Bora's only public beach, and one of Polynesia's most photographed. The water is shallow, the bottom sandy—ideal for swimming.
From Matira, Mount Otemanu (727 m) dominates the landscape. Its basalt summit is Bora Bora's symbol—impossible to miss, it's silhouetted against the sky from anywhere in the lagoon.
The small village of Vaitape stretches along the wharf. A few craft and black pearl shops line the main road. The atmosphere is calm, far from the bustle of resorts on the motus.

Bora Bora still bears the traces of Operation Bobcat. In 1942, 4,000 GIs landed on this island of 1,000 inhabitants to make it a supply base in the Pacific. Eight 7-inch guns and anti-aircraft batteries were installed on the heights.

The Anau guns at Pointe Fitiu are the island's best preserved. A double battery on a reinforced concrete base, a small fort, an ammunition shelter, and a trench network—all restored and explained by trilingual panels installed in 2021.
Continue the island tour through Faanui Bay and its church at the mountain's foot. Two more guns are at Pointe Tereia, accessible by a short trail with views over the motus and overwater bungalows.
The Popoti lookout, a former American radar post on the west coast, offers the best panoramic view of Bora Bora. Access via a steep uphill 4x4 track—on foot or by quad.
At Vaitape wharf, a commemorative plaque recalls the presence of the Seabees (Navy construction battalions). At Motu Mute airport, a timeline traces the history of Operation Bobcat.

Day devoted to Bora Bora's eastern lagoon, less frequented than the Matira side. The Anau site is known for its manta rays—these silent giants with wingspans of 3 to 4 meters come to be cleaned by small fish at a natural cleaning station.

Motu Tapu, a small islet in the south of the lagoon, was used as a setting for a silent film in 1929—Tabu, directed by Murnau. It is a sandbank fringed by a few coconut palms, surrounded by unreal-looking water. It can be admired from the boat.

If you haven't yet done a complete lagoon tour, today's the day. The boat passes over coral gardens between motus, stops for lunch on a deserted islet, and runs along the barrier reef on the ocean side.

activities.text: Lagoon boat tour: coral gardens, swimming with stingrays that aren't very shy, and watching blacktip reef sharks in the shallows between motus. Keep your distance from wildlife.
Sunset from Matira Beach: the sky turns orange and pink while Mount Otemanu stands out in silhouette. Bring a picnic.
Island tour by bike or scooter: the circular road is about 32 km on flat terrain. You pass luxury hotels, fishing villages, and viewpoints over the lagoon.
Outrigger canoe (va'a) outing at sunset. You glide across the lagoon while Otemanu glows red—book for golden hour.
Scuba diving at the Anau site to observe manta rays. Even without certification, supervised introductory dives are offered—you descend to 10–12 meters with an instructor and the rays pass above you.
Late afternoon free on Matira Beach—make the most of it, it's your last day in Bora Bora. The lagoon is especially beautiful late in the day when the low light brings out the shades of blue.
